prompt: After `javac -d out`, where is the class file for `com.example.library.app.Main`?
hint: One directory per part of the name.

choices.text: `out/Main.class`
choices.why: That is where the default package would put it; a package becomes directories.

choices.text: `out/com/example/library/app/Main.class`
choices.why: Right: `find out -type f` listed exactly that path.

choices.text: `out/com.example.library.app.Main.class`
choices.why: The dots become slashes; no file name contains the package.

choices.text: `src/com/example/library/app/Main.class`, beside the source
choices.why: That is where it would go without `-d`; with `-d out` it goes under `out`.

prompt: Standing in `out/com/example/library/app`, Ana ran `java Main` and got `NoClassDefFoundError: Main (wrong name: com/example/library/app/Main)`. What happened?
hint: The file was found. Then it was read.

choices.text: The JVM could not find `Main.class` in the current directory
choices.why: It found it: that is why the error quotes the name written inside the file.

choices.text: It found the file, whose recorded name is the full one
choices.why: Right: a class file knows its package, and is only valid at the path the package spells.

choices.text: The class file was corrupted when `-d` created the directories
choices.why: The same file ran perfectly with `java -cp out com.example.library.app.Main`.

choices.text: `Main` needs `Book`, and `Book` is in another directory
choices.why: The message is about `Main`'s own name, before `Book` is ever needed.

prompt: Why do Java package names start with a domain written backwards, like `com.example`?
hint: Who may use `com.example`?

choices.text: Because the JVM downloads classes from that domain at run time
choices.why: The JVM loads classes from the class path on disk; the name is only a name.

choices.text: So that owners of different domains do not collide on one package name
choices.why: Right: whoever owns the domain owns the names under it.

choices.text: Because `javac` refuses a package that is not a registered domain
choices.why: `javac` checks nothing about domains; `com.example` compiles like any name.

prompt: The JVM looks for classes in the directories and jars listed on the class ___, which `-cp` sets.
hint: Two words; the second is the one missing.

prompt: A colleague moves `Book.java` to the top of `src` and says it still compiles, because `javac src/Book.java src/com/example/library/app/Main.java` works. Who is right about the layout?
hint: What happens when `javac` has to find `Book` instead of being handed it?

choices.text: The colleague: the package line is what counts, and the directory is cosmetic
choices.why: Every tool that has to find a source looks at the directory, as `-sourcepath` showed with three errors.

choices.text: The layout is broken: naming every file on the command line hides it
choices.why: Right: `javac -sourcepath src` failed with `cannot find symbol` until the file went back.

choices.text: Both: `javac` accepts sources anywhere, so nothing will ever fail
choices.why: Maven, an editor and `-sourcepath` all look for the file where the package says it is.

prompt: What does `import java.util.List;` add to the compiled class file?
hint: An import is a promise about short names.

choices.text: A copy of `List`'s code
choices.why: Imports copy nothing; the class file refers to `java.util.List` by name either way.

choices.text: Nothing; it only explains a short name
choices.why: Right: the class file holds full names whether you imported or wrote them out.

choices.text: An instruction to load `java.util` when the program starts
choices.why: Classes are loaded when first used, import or not.

prompt: A file imports `java.util.*` and `java.sql.*` and uses `Date`. What makes it compile with `java.util.Date`?
hint: One kind of import beats another.

choices.text: Putting `import java.util.*;` after `import java.sql.*;`
choices.why: The order of imports decides nothing; both on-demand imports still match.

choices.text: Adding `import static java.util.Date;`
choices.why: A static import is for static members, not for a class.

choices.text: Adding `import java.util.Date;`
choices.why: Right: a single-type import wins over on-demand ones, and the program printed `java.util.Date`.

choices.text: Nothing: the compiler picks the package that was imported first
choices.why: It refused with `reference to Date is ambiguous` and named both.

prompt: Which of these classes can a file use by its short name with no import line at all? Choose all that apply.
hint: One package is imported into every file.

choices.text: `String`
choices.why: Yes: it is in `java.lang`.

choices.text: `Math`
choices.why: Yes: `java.lang.Math`.

choices.text: `List`
choices.why: No: it is `java.util.List`, which needs an import or the full name.

choices.text: `ExecutorService`, after `import java.util.*;`
choices.why: No: it is in `java.util.concurrent`, a different package the `*` does not reach.

prompt: `Modules.java` starts with `import module java.base;`. A teammate compiles it with `--release 21` for an older server. What happens, and why?
hint: When did module imports arrive?

choices.text: It compiles, because `--release` changes only the class file version
choices.why: `--release` also fixes the language level, and the error said module imports need 25.

choices.text: It compiles with a warning, and fails on the server when `List` is first used
choices.why: It does not get that far: `javac` refused at the import line.

choices.text: It fails to compile: module imports need 25
choices.why: Right: `use -source 25 or higher to enable module imports`.

choices.text: It fails because `java.base` does not exist in Java 21
choices.why: `java.base` has existed since Java 9; what is new is importing it.

prompt: Match each import to what it makes available.
hint: The table at the top of the section.

pairs.right: One class, by its short name
Every class of one package, when used
A static member, called without its class

prompt: In the course's layout, where does the source of `com.example.library.App` go?
hint: Maven's source root, then the package.

choices.text: `src/main/java/com/example/library/App.java`
choices.why: Right: `src/main/java` is the root, and the package path follows.

choices.text: `src/com/example/library/App.java`
choices.why: That was section 02's layout for plain `javac`; Maven's root is `src/main/java`.

choices.text: `src/main/java/App.java`, with the package declared inside
choices.why: The package says where the file must be, and Maven looks there.

choices.text: `target/classes/com/example/library/App.java`
choices.why: `target` is what Maven produces and deletes on `clean`; source never goes there.

prompt: Why does the course's `pom.xml` pin a version for every plugin, including ones it never configures?
hint: What would Ubuntu's Maven 3.8.7 use otherwise?

choices.text: Because Maven refuses to build without a version for each plugin
choices.why: Maven builds without them, using its own defaults; that is the problem.

choices.text: Otherwise Maven 3.8.7 runs its own, much older plugins
choices.why: Right: pinned, the old Maven builds exactly what a current one would.

choices.text: To stop the four `Unsafe` warnings that every build prints
choices.why: The warnings come from Maven's own Guava, and nothing in `pom.xml` removes them.

choices.text: So that the first build downloads nothing
choices.why: The first build still downloaded 158 files; pinning decides which versions, not whether.

prompt: How many files did Ana's first build download, according to `grep -c "Downloaded from"`?
hint: The build after it downloaded none.

prompt: Every `mvn` command in the course prints four `WARNING` lines about `sun.misc.Unsafe`. What are they telling you?
hint: Read which jar the second line names.

choices.text: That the project's code uses an internal JDK class it should not
choices.why: The second line names `/usr/share/maven/lib/guava.jar`, part of Maven, not the project.

choices.text: That the build failed and `BUILD SUCCESS` should not be trusted
choices.why: A warning does not stop a build; the verdict is the last lines and the exit status.

choices.text: That Maven's own copy of Guava calls JDK methods that are being retired
choices.why: Right: harmless to the project, and absent when Maven ran on Java 21 in section 05.

prompt: Put the plugins in the order `mvn clean package` ran them.
hint: Clean first, then the phases up to `package`.

prompt: `java -jar target/library-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar` said `no main manifest attribute`. What was missing?
hint: A line in a file inside the jar.

choices.text: The classes: Maven packs only the `pom.xml` until told otherwise
choices.why: `jar tf` listed both classes in the jar.

choices.text: A `Main-Class` line in the manifest
choices.why: Right: the jar plugin wrote it once configured, and `java -jar` started `App`.

choices.text: A `main` method in `App`
choices.why: `App` had one all along; `java -cp target/classes` ran it.

prompt: The second `pom.xml` adds `maven-jar-plugin` under `<plugins>` with no `<version>`. Which version runs?
hint: Which element decides versions?

choices.text: Maven 3.8.7's own default for the jar plugin
choices.why: That is what happens with no pin at all; here `pluginManagement` has one.

choices.text: The newest version on Maven Central
choices.why: Maven never picks the newest on its own; that would make two builds of one commit differ.

choices.text: 3.5.1, the version pinned in `pluginManagement`
choices.why: Right: the manifest said `Created-By: Maven JAR Plugin 3.5.1`.

prompt: A build fails with `Fatal error compiling: error: release version 25 not supported`. `pom.xml` says 25 and `java -version` says 25. What do you check, and what will it probably show?
hint: Maven does not necessarily run on the shell's `java`.

choices.text: `javac -version`, which will show a compiler older than 25
choices.why: The shell's `javac` is not the one Maven used; Maven follows `JAVA_HOME` first.

choices.text: `mvn -v`: it will name an older JDK
choices.why: Right: with `JAVA_HOME` at `default-java`, Maven ran on 21 while the shell's `java` was 25.

choices.text: The compiler plugin's version, which will be too old for 25
choices.why: Pinned at 3.15.0 it compiled for 25 in the same project a moment later.

choices.text: `~/.m2/repository`, which will hold a damaged plugin download
choices.why: A damaged download fails with a resolution error, not a release error.

prompt: `java -cp target/classes com.example.library.App` and `java -jar target/library-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar` both printed the same line. What does each one rely on to find `App`?
hint: One is told the class; the other reads it.

choices.text: Both search every jar under `target` for a `main` method
choices.why: Neither searches; one is given the name and the other reads it from the manifest.

choices.text: The first is given a name and a class path; the second reads the manifest's `Main-Class`
choices.why: Right: and `java -jar` ignores `-cp` entirely.

choices.text: Both read `pom.xml`, which Maven copies next to the classes
choices.why: The copy under `META-INF/maven` is for people; the JVM never reads it.

prompt: Maven keeps every plugin and library it downloads in `~/.m2/___`, and a second build finds them there.
hint: The local one, as opposed to Maven Central.
